solutions.check: 32 entries verified against the grid (lengths, crossings, linked-clue mapping)

clue.text: Performance of an arse loosely enthralling one

indicators.note: to enthral is to hold captive

parts.note: rectal = of the rectum, which is 'an arse' if you speak loosely

explanation.surface: A review of some show that consisted of a backside being waggled about.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Loosely' is not an anagram signal here: it apologises for glossing 'rectal' as 'of an arse'. RECT(I)AL is the whole trick.
explanation.definitionFit: A recital is a performance, typically of music or poetry.

clue.text: see 18ac.
(& 24dn.) Fail to separate oddballs, as Republicans do around Trump

explanation.surface: A jibe that Republicans cannot bring themselves to split from the eccentrics around Trump.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fail to separate' reads as one phrase meaning 'stay together', uncomfortably close to the answer's own sense, but the break falls after 'Fail'. The definition is a description, not a dictionary synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: To close ranks is to unite in mutual defence, which is what a party does around a leader under attack.

clue.text: Mean Bottom or Scrooge?

explanation.surface: A question of whether some miser is Bottom, the weaver from A Midsummer Night's Dream, or Scrooge.
explanation.walkthrough: Capital B makes 'Bottom' look like Shakespeare's character, but it is just a backside. 'Tightarse' is British slang for a skinflint.
explanation.definitionFit: Scrooge, Dickens's miser, is the archetypal tightarse.

clue.text: Lords chief dodgy 'cure' for dishonest gain

indicators.note: chief means the head or leading letter of the word Lords is taken
dodgy means unreliable or crooked, so the letters of cure are jumbled

explanation.surface: A satirical jab at peers whose leader offers a shady remedy in return for money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lords chief' reads like a title, but 'chief' just takes the first letter of Lords; 'dodgy' then rearranges CURE.
explanation.definitionFit: Lucre is money, especially when gained by greedy or underhand means, as in 'filthy lucre'.

clue.text: Bribe returned — Davey was affected?

parts.note: a sop = something given to buy someone off
Ed Davey, leader of the Liberal Democrats

explanation.surface: A bribe handed back, and a question about whether the Lib Dem leader was influenced by it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Affected' suggests 'influenced' by the bribe; here it means putting on airs. Ed Davey is a British party leader, the Liberal Democrats' head.
explanation.definitionFit: To pose is to behave affectedly, so 'posed' = 'was affected'.

clue.text: The game of Roger Roger

parts.note: to roger and to poke are both slang for having sex
'Roger' is the old radio code word for R

explanation.surface: A teasing reference to what Roger Roger likes to play, as though that were his name.
explanation.walkthrough: The doubled name looks like a comic person; the first Roger is the slang verb, the second the radio word for R.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: poker is one card game among many, and 'The game' reads as the one Roger plays.

clue.text: Government aimed to ditch a communiqué

parts.note: the state is the government of a country

indicators.note: to ditch means to drop, so a letter is thrown out of the word before

parts.note: aimed means meant, as in intended

explanation.surface: A government meant to scrap a public announcement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'aimed' looks like part of the government's plan, but it is a synonym in the past tense; 'to ditch a' then drops one letter from it.
explanation.definitionFit: A communiqué is an official announcement, the same as a formal statement issued to the press.

clue.text: Part inside testicles — can't stand

indicators.note: the answer is part of the words that follow

explanation.surface: A complaint that some part of the anatomy down there is unbearable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Inside' looks like the signal to look within, but it is the fodder: the answer straddles 'inside' and 'testicles'.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiom: 'can't stand' is everyday speech for loathing, the same strong dislike the verb names.

clue.text: In canteen, handy for the boozer

definitions.note: an adjective phrase standing for a noun: something handy for the boozer

parts.note: a canteen is also a water bottle carried by soldiers or campers

explanation.surface: A tip that the works canteen is conveniently close to the pub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Canteen' suggests a dining hall and 'boozer' a pub, but a canteen is also a drinking bottle and the boozer is a drinker. 'In' is the adjective 'fashionable', not a preposition.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by description: a small spirits flask kept in a hip pocket is always to hand for a drinker.

clue.text: Cream on goolies — inside, not on the outside

indicators.note: the answer sits inside the words before it, spanning three of them

explanation.surface: Instructions for applying ointment to the testicles: rub it in, don't leave it on top.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as application advice; 'goolies' is British slang for testicles.
explanation.definitionFit: Loose synonym: to be among a crowd is to be in its midst, not on its outside edge.

clue.text: Cats start to tongue Harry which encourages mouse activity

indicators.note: the start of a word is its first letter

parts.note: to harry = to bait, to torment

explanation.surface: Cats teasing and licking at something that gets the mice moving.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is all cat and mouse; 'mouse activity' is really clicking a computer mouse. 'Harry' is the verb, not a name.
explanation.definitionFit: Clickbait is online content designed to make readers click on a link.

clue.text: His Majesty's now possibly pissed at three

indicators.note: British slang for drunk, so the letters stagger into a new order

explanation.surface: The King may be drunk by three in the afternoon.
explanation.walkthrough: His Majesty's is a London West End theatre, renamed from Her Majesty's after the Queen died; 'now' points to the new name and 'possibly' marks it as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: His Majesty's in the Haymarket is one London playhouse, and 'possibly' flags it as just one instance.

clue.text: Labour might require such a device as sticking Penny in the military!

definitions.text: Labour might require such a device

indicators.note: sticking one thing in another means pushing it inside, as a pin is stuck in a cushion
'in the military' says where Penny goes: within the word for the armed forces

explanation.surface: A political quip that the Labour Party needs a device like putting Penny into the armed forces.
explanation.walkthrough: Capital L makes 'Labour' the party; it is childbirth. Penny Mordaunt, a Navy reservist and Conservative minister, is the likely surface target.
explanation.definitionFit: Forceps are the tongs used to help deliver a baby during labour.

clue.text: Dicky, on going arse over tip, gets tender

explanation.surface: Someone called Dicky takes a tumble and ends up sore.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dicky' looks like a name and 'tender' like a bruise; 'arse over tip' is British for head over heels.
explanation.definitionFit: To tender is to offer, as in tendering a bid or resignation.

clue.text: A senior, given time, gets caught in fact, in 'flagrante' –"marvellous!"

indicators.note: gets caught in means these letters are trapped inside the jumbled phrase
'in flagrante' suggests something caught in the act and in disarray, so the letters of fact and in are scrambled

parts.note: S is a standard abbreviation for senior

explanation.surface: An older person caught red-handed in the act, with the onlooker exclaiming in delight.
explanation.walkthrough: The Latin phrase 'in flagrante' (caught in the act) is split: its 'in' joins the fodder and 'flagrante', suggesting blazing disorder, signals the rearrangement; 'gets caught in' then places the senior's letters inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Fantastic as an exclamation is enthusiastic praise, a synonym for marvellous or wonderful.

clue.text: House cover-up is effected by one old PM

definitions.text: House cover-up is effected by one
definitions.meaning: the cover-up is a straw or reed roof, and 'one' is the craftsman who lays it
a former British Prime Minister, here the Conservative leader of 1979-90

explanation.surface: A former prime minister is behind a scandal about the House.
explanation.walkthrough: 'House cover-up' sounds like a parliamentary scandal; it is a roof, and the one who puts it on is a thatcher.
explanation.definitionFit: Margaret Thatcher was Prime Minister of the UK.

clue.text: Arse wobbled in true style, darling

indicators.note: wobbled = shaken about, and ARSE is jumbled in with TRUE

explanation.surface: An appreciative remark to someone whose bottom wobbles in a truly stylish way.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a leering compliment; all eight letters of ARSE and TRUE are shaken together.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Treasure' is an endearment, like darling.

clue.text: Like a strict TT, stony, son-of-a-bitch, eastern Republican

explanation.surface: A string of insults for a hard-hearted, puritanical Republican from the East.
explanation.walkthrough: TT is short for teetotaller, not the Isle of Man motorcycle race.
explanation.definitionFit: A strict teetotaller is always stone-cold sober.

clue.text: TV etc showing recurring image: ex-royal Alexandra's butt

parts.note: Princess Diana, formerly of the royal family

indicators.note: the butt is the end, so the last letter of Alexandra

explanation.surface: Television keeps running a picture of a former royal's bottom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ex-royal Alexandra' reads as one person; the ex-royal is Di and Alexandra only gives up her last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: TV is one branch of the mass media, and 'etc' widens it to press and radio.

clue.text: (& 1dn.) Balls possibly in line of fire from such an unthinking response?

definitions.text: Balls possibly in line of fire
definitions.meaning: read literally: a groin is exactly where an upward-jerking knee lands
read as meant: a reflex response, the one a doctor tests by tapping below the kneecap

explanation.surface: A warning that someone's testicles are in the path of a reflex.
explanation.walkthrough: The joke takes 'knee-jerk' literally: a knee flying up makes the groin the target. The phrase itself means an automatic, unconsidered reaction.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiom: the automatic kick of the patellar reflex became the standard phrase for any response made without thought.

clue.text: Strip clubs inside bar entrance

indicators.note: 'clubs inside' means the clubs letter is placed within the strip

parts.note: a lath is a thin strip of wood

explanation.surface: Directions to the strip clubs found just inside a pub's door.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strip clubs' is a single phrase in the surface; split it, and 'bar entrance' becomes a verb phrase, not a pub door.
explanation.definitionFit: To latch a door is to fasten it, barring the entrance.

clue.text: Flash's uniform accommodating large body

indicators.note: to accommodate is to give room to, as a hotel houses guests, so the large body sits within the uniform

parts.note: flat = uniform, as in a flat rate
the UN, a large international body

explanation.surface: Flash, the comic-book hero or the cad, has a costume roomy enough for a big physique.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Uniform' suggests a costume or the letter U; here it is FLAT, and 'large body' is the United Nations.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: to flash your wealth is to display it showily, just as you would parade it.

clue.text: For sale: kinky casual wear

indicators.note: twisted, so the letters are bent into a new order

explanation.surface: A small ad offering fetish gear that is comfortable enough to wear every day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Kinky' sets up a naughty listing; loafers are slip-on shoes.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: laceless slip-on shoes are a staple of relaxed, off-duty dress.

clue.text: Guardsman finally eases off penetration

indicators.note: off means that letter is removed from the guard's word

parts.note: a sentry is a soldier keeping guard

indicators.note: finally means take the closing letter of the word eases

explanation.surface: A soldier on duty at last relaxes, with a smutty hint for Private Eye readers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'finally' points at eases, not Guardsman: its last letter S is what comes 'off' SENTRY.
explanation.definitionFit: An entry is the act of going in, so penetration is a fair synonym, with a nudge at the double meaning.

clue.text: Speaker's stand on unstable sort being introduced to drink

indicators.note: being introduced to means the jumbled letters are placed inside the drink
unstable means shaky or disordered, so the letters of sort are rearranged

explanation.surface: A wobbly sort of person is given a drink before taking the speaker's platform.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on' is only a link here, and 'Speaker' with a capital suggests the Commons, but any public speaker's platform fits.
explanation.definitionFit: A rostrum is a raised platform on which a public speaker stands.

clue.text: Rooftop game: letting bastard go

indicators.note: 'letting … go' means releasing, so the bastard's letter is let out of the game
completes 'letting … go', to release

parts.note: b = bastard, as in the abbreviated expletive

explanation.surface: A rooftop game being played until some rotter is allowed to leave.
explanation.walkthrough: B for bastard is the abbreviation used in printed swearing ('you b——').
explanation.definitionFit: The ridge is the top edge of a roof.

clue.text: see 2dn.
Turned out lousy, being in need of instruction

indicators.note: poor, bad, so the letters are in a poor order

explanation.surface: Someone did badly because they had never been taught properly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turned out' looks like the anagram indicator; it is the fodder, and 'lousy' does the rearranging.
explanation.definitionFit: Loose synonym: someone never taught lacks schooling and so still needs lessons.

clue.text: Screwed on entering appropriate place?

indicators.note: to enter is to go into, so 'on' goes into the bed

parts.note: bed is the appropriate place for screwing

explanation.surface: A question of whether some act of penetration took place in the right spot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Appropriate place' is a cheeky cryptic hint for BED, fitting the definition's sense.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Boned' is slang for having had sex, i.e. screwed.

clue.text: Only recently painted as tasteless?

definitions.meaning: fresh paint has not dried and is still slightly sticky

explanation.surface: A sniffy remark that a newly decorated room is in poor taste.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface pairs the two meanings as though one explained the other: the room is tacky in both senses.
explanation.definitionFit: Tacky means tasteless and cheap-looking.

clue.text: Entrepreneur (as Ian?) protects massive land area

indicators.note: the phrase holds the answer within it, guarding it

explanation.surface: A businessman, perhaps one called Ian, looks after a huge territory.
explanation.walkthrough: The bracketed aside looks like a name guess; it is there to supply the hidden letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Eurasia, Europe and Asia together, is the largest land mass.
